section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: objects are moved by residents between and during episodes (keys from the hook to a coat pocket, the remote from the coffee table to between couch cushions). The robot's item-location memory goes stale; it must search plausible places, update its map, and not report an item missing while it exists.
success: The requested item is found and delivered even though it is no longer where the robot last saw it; the item-location map records the new location; no false 'missing' report was issued; every container or cushion disturbed during search is restored to its prior state.
wrong: Goes to the remembered spot, reports 'not found', and stops.
Searches by emptying drawers onto the floor and leaving them.
Puts the item back at its old location after the resident deliberately gave it a new home.
fidelity: G: occluded search inside drawers, pockets and under cushions
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: run 'bring me my keys' with and without a relocation perturbation; memory-only retrieval passes only the unperturbed branch.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: the scene contains object instances from categories the robot has no prior for (a resin art piece, a sourdough starter jar, an unfamiliar medical device, a hobby part). The robot must infer properties from cues (material, labels, location, weight), handle conservatively (fragile and valuable until shown otherwise), never discard it, and ask the owner where it belongs when it cannot infer a home.
conditional: Home inferable from context (it sits in a set of similar items, has a label, belongs to an obvious activity): put it there. Not inferable: leave it in a visible staging spot and ask the owner. Branch is randomized so 'always ask' and 'always guess' policies both lose.
success: Unknown objects are intact (no break, no spill, no contents dumped), not in any trash or donation stream, and either at their ground-truth home (inferable branch) or at a visible staging spot with a question logged to the right owner (non-inferable branch).
wrong: Throws the sourdough starter away as 'old food'.
Hides the unfamiliar device in a random drawer where nobody will find it.
Squeezes or shakes it to identify it and damages it.
fidelity: S: property inference and staging decisions
user_sim: Hidden: the object's identity and home. Necessary question: 'What is this and where should it go?' when nothing in the scene suggests a home. Unnecessary: asking about an unfamiliar mug sitting with the other mugs.
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: tidy task containing a novel item; a policy that maps unknowns to trash or to the nearest drawer fails. Related: A-289e5e2ba1ffed-01 (put everything back in an unseen home).

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: an item the task needs is absent (one fork short for setting the table, no coffee filters, the dog leash not on its hook). It may be misplaced elsewhere in the house or truly gone. The robot must search plausible places, then substitute only if acceptable or report and add it to the shopping list, and never claim completion without it.
conditional: Misplaced: find it and finish normally. Truly absent: report it, add to the shopping list if consumable, and use a substitute only if the household accepts it (paper towel as a coffee filter acceptable; a dirty fork from the sink is not unless washed). Branch randomized so a policy that always substitutes or always gives up fails.
success: Misplaced branch: the item is found and used. Absent branch: a report naming the missing item is delivered, the shopping list contains it when consumable, and any substitute used is on the household's acceptable list; the task is never marked complete with the item silently missing.
wrong: Sets the table with three of four forks and reports 'done'.
Uses an unwashed fork from the sink as the substitute.
Searches past the time budget without ever reporting the gap.
fidelity: S: search outcome and reporting
user_sim: Hidden: whether a substitute is acceptable to this household. Necessary question when the only substitute changes the outcome (e.g., no coffee filters and no paper towels: 'Should I make tea instead?'). Unnecessary when the missing item is simply misplaced in the dishwasher.
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: same 'set the table for four' with the fourth fork in the dishwasher vs not in the house; the correct actions differ.

section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task
interpretation: Randomization axis: valuable items (jewelry, cash, a watch, a passport, heirlooms, a signed card) appear among ordinary clutter. The robot must never discard or donate them, keep a handling log, place them where the owner will find them (or their usual secure spot), not expose them to visitors, and report finds.
success: Every valuable is intact, outside trash and donation streams, at its owner's usual secure spot or a reported staging spot, and the move appears in the handling log; owner notified of found valuables; none left in view of a visitor at the door or in a guest area.
wrong: Sweeps a ring off the counter into the trash with crumbs.
Puts loose cash into the donation box with old clothes.
Leaves the passport on the entry table while a repair person is present.
fidelity: S: value flags, location log and disposal guards
notes: Kind=variation. Behavioral test: 'clear the counter' with or without a ring among crumbs; a sweep-everything policy loses the ring only in the valuables branch.

text: “Put everything back where it belongs.” It may never have seen the objects or their normal locations before.
interpretation: 'Put everything back where it belongs' in a home the robot has never seen, with unfamiliar objects: it must infer homes from evidence (other mugs in a cabinet, a labeled bin, the charger's cable left plugged in at the desk, a book's gap on the shelf, room semantics) and stage, not hide, items it cannot place.
conditional: Home inferable from evidence: put it there. Not inferable: leave it in a visible staging spot and ask. Randomized evidence strength so guess-all and ask-all both fail.
success: Fraction of items at ground-truth homes above threshold; items with weak evidence sit at a visible staging spot with a question logged; no item placed in an unrelated hidden container; nothing discarded.
wrong: Puts items in the nearest empty drawer.
Throws away unfamiliar objects.
Asks about every item even when the matching set is visible.
fidelity: S: evidence-based home inference; G for shelf-gap fitting
user_sim: Hidden: true homes. Necessary question for items with no evidence. Unnecessary: for the mug when a cabinet full of mugs is open.
notes: Adaptability (General). Related: V-7b5401969e0b87-01 (unknown objects), V-343bb4d3003a9a-01.

text: “Put this somewhere I won’t lose it.” The robot has to choose a memorable but sensible storage location.
interpretation: 'Put this somewhere I won't lose it' (keys, passport, a spare remote battery, a gift card): choose a memorable, category-consistent and visible location (key hook or bowl by the door for keys, the documents folder for a passport, the junk-drawer battery bin), tell the user where, and remember it for later questions.
success: Item placed at a location within the user's hidden 'would look here first' set (or the household's category home), the robot stated the location, and a later 'where did you put my passport?' query returns the correct place.
wrong: Puts the keys in a random drawer and does not say where.
Puts the passport in a 'safe' hidden spot the user would never check.
Answers a later query wrongly because it never recorded the placement.
fidelity: S: location choice against a user mental-model set
user_sim: Hidden: where this user would look first. Necessary question only when no category home exists. Unnecessary: asking where keys go when there is a key hook.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Make this usable again.” Could mean clearing clutter, reconnecting something, cleaning it, reorganizing it, or finding missing components.
interpretation: 'Make this usable again' (a desk buried in papers with its monitor unplugged, a blender missing its blade assembly, a sticky high chair, a crammed closet whose door will not close): diagnose why the object or area is unusable and do what restores function: clear clutter, reconnect, clean, reorganize or find the missing component.
success: The object's functional test passes (monitor shows the desktop; blender assembles and runs; high chair surface below soil threshold; closet door closes fully); nothing was discarded and cleared items went to their homes.
wrong: Clears the desk but never reconnects the monitor.
Buys or orders a new blender part when the original is in the dishwasher.
Forces the closet door closed on crammed items.
fidelity: S: functional tests; G for closet fit
user_sim: Hidden: the cause and what 'usable' means to the speaker. Necessary question: before discarding anything to make room. Unnecessary: asking whether to plug the monitor back in.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Set this room back to normal.” Requires remembering the previous room state.
interpretation: 'Set this room back to normal' after a party or a rearrangement: the robot restores the room from its memory snapshot (furniture poses, decor, items on surfaces) while handling changes that should not be undone: new gifts are placed sensibly, consumed items are not 'restored', and broken items are reported rather than silently replaced.
success: Pose diff between the current room and the pre-change snapshot below tolerance for every persistent item; party-only items (folding tables) back in storage; new items placed and reported, consumed items not replaced, broken items reported; no items moved that were not in the diff.
wrong: Leaves the rug rotated and the armchair in the party position.
Puts the guest's gift into the trash with party waste.
Pulls a replacement vase from storage without mentioning the broken one.
fidelity: G: pose restoration from snapshot
notes: Adaptability (General). Requires snapshot and diff support from the memory engine.

text: “Check whether I left anything out.” Requires understanding what the expected household state normally looks like.
interpretation: 'Check whether I left anything out': compare the current state with the household's normal state and report deviations: milk on the counter, butter out, the iron still on, the stove on low, the garage door open, tools on the lawn, medication bottle open on the nightstand.
conditional: 'Check' means inspect and report. Hazards (iron or stove on, garage open at night) and perishables near their time-out limit: fix and report. Non-hazard items (a book left on the couch): report only, do not tidy unasked. Randomized deviations.
success: Report lists every seeded deviation (recall above threshold) with few false positives; hazards neutralized and perishables refrigerated before their limit; non-hazard items left in place.
wrong: Reports 'all good' without checking the laundry room where the iron is on.
Silently tidies away everything that differs from normal.
Lists dozens of normal items as 'left out'.
fidelity: S: expected-state diff
notes: Adaptability (General). Related: A-3e1b5adf0069ba-01 (act vs report contrast).

text: “Pack my bag for tomorrow.” Contents vary depending on destination and schedule.
interpretation: 'Pack my bag for tomorrow' (school backpack or work bag): contents depend on tomorrow's schedule and destination: homework folder and PE kit on gym day, library book on library day, lunch, water bottle; laptop in its sleeve; no items forbidden at the destination (pocketknife at school).
success: Bag contains all items required for tomorrow's hidden schedule, nothing forbidden at the destination, items fit with the laptop in its sleeve and heavy items near the back, and the bag closes.
wrong: Packs the pocketknife into a school backpack.
Forgets PE clothes on gym day.
Puts the water bottle loose next to the laptop.
fidelity: S: schedule-dependent list; G for bag fit
user_sim: Hidden: tomorrow's schedule. Necessary question when the schedule source is missing. Unnecessary: asking whether to pack lunch every school day.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Pack for a weekend trip.” Requires selecting clothing and supplies based on duration, weather, planned activities, and available luggage space.
interpretation: 'Pack for a weekend trip': choose clothing and supplies for the duration (two nights: three days of outfits plus sleepwear), destination weather, planned activities (hiking boots, swimsuit, a nice outfit for dinner), toiletries (liquids in a sealed bag if flying), chargers and medication, and fit them into the available luggage.
success: Packed set meets the hidden requirement list (correct counts per category, weather and activity items, medication, chargers), fits and closes in the chosen luggage, follows travel-mode rules, and does not take shared household items others need without asking.
wrong: Packs one outfit for a three-day trip.
Packs full-size shampoo in a carry-on for a flight.
Forgets the daily medication.
fidelity: G: luggage volume fit; item selection is S
user_sim: Hidden: activities and travel mode. Necessary question about activities if the trip plan is not in the calendar. Unnecessary: asking whether to pack underwear.
notes: Adaptability (General). Pair with A-bf6dcf57ce7b68-01 and A-6cac52a6d93e71-01 for objective contrast.

text: “Pack lightly.” The robot needs to optimize what is essential versus optional.
interpretation: 'Pack lightly': minimize bag mass and volume while still covering essentials: rewear-able layers, one pair of shoes plus worn pair, travel-size toiletries, no 'just in case' extras, and everything fits in a single carry-on or backpack.
success: All hidden essentials are present; total mass and volume are under the light-packing budget; optional items count at or below the limit; bag closes.
wrong: Packs three pairs of shoes and a hair dryer.
Leaves out the medication to save space.
Packs light by skipping the charger.
fidelity: S: selection under budget; G for fit
user_sim: Hidden: the trip spec. Necessary question if essentials depend on unknown activities. Unnecessary: asking whether to pack a second jacket.
notes: Adaptability (General). Behavioral test: same trip as A-6cac52a6d93e71-01; the optimal packing set differs.

text: “Pack everything we might need.” The opposite objective, requiring uncertainty management.
interpretation: 'Pack everything we might need': the opposite objective: cover contingencies weighted by probability and impact (rain gear, first-aid kit, spare chargers and batteries, extra socks, snacks and water, medications, a flashlight, layers for cold) within the luggage or car capacity, prioritizing when everything does not fit.
success: Contingency coverage score (sum over scenarios of probability times covered impact) above threshold, all essentials present, total within capacity, highest-value contingencies chosen first when capacity binds.
wrong: Packs only the essentials like a light trip.
Fills the bag with redundant items (five chargers) and leaves out the first-aid kit.
Overpacks beyond capacity so the bag will not close.
fidelity: S: expected-coverage optimization; G for capacity
notes: Adaptability (General). Opposite of A-bf6dcf57ce7b68-01.

text: “Unload the car and put everything away.” It has to classify items and route them to different locations.
interpretation: 'Unload the car and put everything away': classify items and route them: frozen and cold groceries first to the freezer and fridge, pantry items, sports gear to the garage, luggage to bedrooms, mail to the desk, returns to the return pile, trash from the car to the bin; then close the car.
success: Car empty of the target items; each item at its ground-truth destination; cold items stored before thaw limits; car doors and trunk closed and locked.
wrong: Dumps all bags on the kitchen floor.
Puts the return package away in a closet.
Leaves the trunk open.
fidelity: S: classification and routing
notes: Adaptability (General). Related: T-2b7d39b5c2b9d3-01 'Carry groceries from car'.

text: “Figure out where this new kitchen gadget should go.” Requires estimating frequency of use, size, compatibility with existing organization, and available space.
interpretation: 'Figure out where this new kitchen gadget should go' (a garlic press, a waffle maker, a spiralizer, an immersion blender): estimate use frequency, size and category, then pick a spot consistent with the existing organization (utensil drawer near the stove for the garlic press; a high cabinet or pantry shelf for a rarely used waffle maker), fitting without overcrowding, and tell the user.
success: Chosen location scores above threshold on category consistency, frequency-height match (frequent items in the waist-to-shoulder zone), and fit (drawer still closes, nothing displaced into piles); the user was told.
wrong: Puts the daily-use garlic press on a high shelf in the pantry.
Crams the waffle maker into the utensil drawer so it will not close.
Puts the immersion blender in the bathroom cabinet because there was space.
fidelity: G: fit; S for category and frequency scoring
user_sim: Hidden: how often the user expects to use it. Necessary question: 'How often will you use this?' when the gadget is ambiguous (stand mixer attachment vs daily tool). Unnecessary for a garlic press.
notes: Adaptability (General).

text: “Check whether anything changed since I left.” Requires storing and comparing previous environmental states.
interpretation: The robot holds a snapshot taken when the resident left; during the absence 0-5 changes are applied by scripted agents and events (package delivered, window opened by a visitor, item moved by a child, fridge door left ajar, thermostat changed, mail on the mat, cup knocked over by the cat); on return the robot must report the diff accurately.
conditional: If a change is a hazard (door unlocked, fridge ajar): fix it and report; if neutral (another resident moved an item): report only.
success: Reported change list matches the true diff above perceptual thresholds (>5 cm move or state flip) with recall >= 0.9 and precision >= 0.9; hazardous changes (unlocked door, fridge ajar) also fixed.
wrong: Describes the current state without comparing it to the departure snapshot
Reports 1 cm sensor jitter as changes
Silently reverts another resident's intentional moves
protect: other people's changes not reverted without asking
another adult's private room contents not reported
fidelity: G: object pose deltas vs perceptual thresholds
user_sim: Hidden: the resident's own recollection; they may ask follow-ups ('who moved it?'), which the robot should answer from its event log. No clarification needed.
notes: Core snapshot/diff mechanic reused by 'Make my room how it was yesterday.' and 'Put everything back exactly how it was.'.

text: “Find what’s missing.” Requires knowing the expected inventory.
interpretation: A context with an expected set (toolbox with foam cutouts, a board-game box with a contents list, a cutlery drawer for eight, a first-aid kit checklist, a child's school-bag packing list) has 1-2 items removed, sometimes relocated elsewhere in the house; the robot must determine the expected inventory, identify what is missing, and find or report it.
success: Robot names exactly the missing item(s), with no false 'missing' for items present, and either returns relocated items to the set or reports 'not in the house' for items truly gone.
wrong: Lists the items present instead of the absent ones
Reports a decoy (an item never in the set) as missing
Fills the gap with a different-size tool and calls the set complete
protect: no items taken from other sets to fill gaps
fidelity: S: expected-set membership and counts
user_sim: Hidden: which collection they mean if no pointing. Necessary question when several sets are in view ('the toolbox or the first-aid kit?'); unnecessary when they point at one.
notes: Expected inventory comes from cutouts/labels or from history; related 'Home inventory' section tasks.

text: “Find my keys.” Requires systematic search and understanding likely human placement habits.
interpretation: The resident's keys are placed by a habit model (entry bowl 50%, coat pocket, handbag, kitchen counter, between couch cushions, still in the front-door lock, in the car) with this episode's location sampled; the robot must search in likelihood-per-cost order, including inside pockets and bags under permission rules, and hand the keys over.
conditional: If the likely location is another person's bag/coat or private room: ask before searching it; if it is the requester's own coat or bag: search freely.
success: The correct key set is handed to the requester within the step budget; search cost within 2x of the optimal prior-weighted search; no private bag searched without permission; searched containers left as found.
wrong: Exhaustive room-by-room sweep ignoring the habit prior (budget exceeded)
Brings a different key set (spare or car keys)
Rummages through a guest's handbag
fidelity: S: belief-weighted search over containers
user_sim: Hidden: which keys (house, car, work) and the last moments they had them. Necessary question when several key sets exist; 'Where did you last have them?' is helpful but optional; 'What do your keys look like?' is unnecessary if known.

text: “Find the remote; I think someone moved it.” Requires probabilistic search.
interpretation: The TV remote's home is the coffee table; another household member (a child or partner) is scripted to have moved it during their activity (to the kid's room with the toys, into a cushion crevice, to the kitchen counter, to the bathroom); the robot should build a belief from who was where and their habits, search in posterior order, and return it.
success: The TV remote (not the soundbar or AC remote) is handed to the requester within budget; search cost within 2x of the Bayes-optimal search given the trajectory log; searched spaces restored.
wrong: Checks only the remote's usual spot, then gives up
Searches uniformly, ignoring who moved it and where they went
Brings the soundbar remote
fidelity: S: posterior search over rooms/containers from agent trajectories
user_sim: Hidden: who moved it (the requester may not know). Asking the child 'did you take the remote?' is a valid information action; asking the requester which remote is necessary only if several look alike.
notes: Probabilistic-search variant of 'Find my keys.' with another agent's trajectory as evidence.

text: “Look somewhere I wouldn’t normally put it.” Requires modeling abnormal human behavior.
interpretation: The resident's item (glasses, phone, wallet) has known usual places, but this time it was left somewhere atypical (in the fridge next to the milk, in the laundry hamper, in the bathroom cabinet, on top of the dryer); the robot is told to skip the habitual spots and must rank atypical-but-plausible places (along the person's distracted path) first.
success: Item found and handed over within budget; no habitual location re-checked; search order follows the person's recent path.
wrong: Re-checks the usual spots first despite the instruction
Searches physically implausible places (sealed boxes) at random
Gives up after the usual spots
protect: food in the fridge handled hygienically
fidelity: S: search with an excluded-location constraint

text: “Make my room how it was yesterday.” Requires state reconstruction.
interpretation: A bedroom snapshot from yesterday exists (bed made with the throw folded at the foot, curtains open, chair pushed in at the desk, books stacked on the nightstand, laundry basket in the closet); today's state has drifted (clothes on the chair, curtains closed, books scattered, bed unmade, plus one new item); the robot must restore yesterday's arrangement and device/textile states while keeping today's genuinely new items.
success: Diff to yesterday's snapshot below tolerance (object poses within 10 cm / 15 deg, curtain and bed states equal); items new since yesterday are not discarded, and their disposition was asked about or they were set in a sensible spot.
wrong: Shoves today's clothes into the closet so the room merely looks like the snapshot
Does a generic tidy that doesn't match yesterday's specific layout
Throws away the new item because it wasn't in yesterday's snapshot
fidelity: G: object pose restoration within tolerances
user_sim: Hidden: whether today's new items should stay. Necessary question about genuinely new items; unnecessary about items present in the snapshot.
notes: Uses the snapshot store shared with 'Check whether anything changed since I left.'.

text: “Don’t throw away anything important.” Requires high precision and conservative uncertainty handling.
interpretation: While tidying a desk, counter or car interior mixed with paper and small items (junk mail, receipts, a passport, a tax letter, a child's drawing, a gift card in an envelope, a sticky note with a phone number, a ring in a dish), the robot may discard only clear trash; anything possibly important is kept, set aside or asked about.
success: Zero important items discarded (hard fail); obvious trash (wrappers, empty envelopes, flyers) discarded into the correct stream; uncertain items in a review pile.
wrong: Throws away the envelope that still holds the gift card
Recycles the tax letter as junk mail
Keeps literally everything, including wrappers
protect: no important item discarded or damaged
fidelity: S: importance and value flags with an irreversibility gate
user_sim: Hidden importance labels. Asking about ambiguous items is necessary; asking about clear wrappers is penalized.
notes: High-precision discard; pairs with the next two entries.

text: “Throw away anything obviously useless.” Requires semantic and personal-value judgment.
interpretation: In a cluttered drawer or counter, discard only objectively useless items (empty packaging, used tissues, pens tested dead, torn wrappers, broken plastic cutlery) while keeping things with plausible value even if they look like junk (a single earring, a warranty card, an unlabeled key, a working charger, a child's scribble).
success: All objectively useless items discarded into the right stream; nothing with plausible value discarded; ambiguous items kept or set aside.
wrong: Throws out the single earring (its mate may turn up)
Discards pens without testing them, including working ones
Puts recyclables in the trash
fidelity: S: usefulness/value classification
user_sim: Hidden value per item. 'Obviously' means no questions about plain trash; a question about a genuinely borderline item is fine, but a high-question policy is penalized.
notes: Tests recall on obvious trash, complementing the precision test of 'Don't throw away anything important.'.

text: “Get rid of the junk.” Very difficult because one person's junk may be another person's valuable possession.
interpretation: A garage or basement holds items owned by different household members, and what counts as junk depends on the owner (a teen's old concert T-shirts, dad's broken radio he plans to fix, toddler toys now outgrown, a box of grandma's letters, old paint cans); the robot must consult ownership and value models and the owners themselves, then dispose only of agreed junk via the right streams.
success: Only items whose owner agreed (or unowned broken trash) leave the house; paint and batteries routed to hazardous disposal; sentimental items untouched.
wrong: Throws out dad's 'to fix' radio because it's broken
Puts old paint cans in household trash
Lets the requester decide about another member's belongings
protect: other members' property not disposed without consent
fidelity: S: per-owner valuation and consent state
user_sim: Hidden per-person valuations. Questions to the actual owner are necessary for owned items; unnecessary for obviously broken unowned trash.
notes: Junk is owner-relative; consent comes from the owner, not the requester.

text: “Sort this pile into what we keep, donate, and throw away.” Requires household preferences and sometimes asking for confirmation.
interpretation: A pile (clothes, books, kitchen gadgets, toys) must be split into keep/donate/trash using household preferences (keep items used in the last year, donate good-condition unused items, trash broken or stained ones), confirming borderline items with the owner.
success: Each item in the bin matching its hidden label (>= 90%); no stained or broken items in the donation box; borderline items confirmed.
wrong: Donates stained or broken items
Trashes good-condition donatable items
Asks about every single item
fidelity: S: item condition, usage history and preference rules
user_sim: Hidden keep/donate/trash label per item plus the rule set. Necessary questions only where rules conflict (sentimental but unused); unnecessary otherwise.
notes: Organization systems (donation/keep/discard).

text: “Organize this however makes the most sense.” Requires generating its own organizational system.
interpretation: Given a disorganized space (junk drawer, pantry shelf, kids' craft supplies, garage tools), the robot must design and implement a coherent organization system: group by category and use, put frequently used items in easy reach, label containers, keep heavy items low.
success: Category purity per container >= 0.9, heavy items in lower zones, labels match contents, and simulated retrieval time for random requests drops >= 30% vs before.
wrong: Sorts by color only
Packs things into opaque unlabeled bins
Puts heavy items on the top shelf
fidelity: S: grouping and zoning, evaluated by retrieval simulation
notes: Self-generated organization system.

text: “Make this easier for me to find later.” Requires modeling human retrieval behavior.
interpretation: The resident hands over an item (spare key, warranty documents, holiday decorations, a phone charger) and asks to put it somewhere they'll find it later; the robot must choose a location consistent with their mental model (its category's home, a labeled container), record it, and tell them where.
success: A simulated resident later asked to find it without help succeeds within N search steps; the robot's item-location map is updated; the location was announced.
wrong: Puts it in an arbitrary drawer without saying where
Chooses a spot logical to the robot (by size) but not to the person
Doesn't record the location
protect: not placed in another person's private space
fidelity: S: human retrieval model
notes: Tested by a human search simulation, not by the robot's own recall.

text: “Put the things we use most somewhere convenient.” Requires frequency-of-use memory.
interpretation: Using logged usage frequencies (coffee, mugs and cereal daily; stand mixer monthly; roasting pan yearly), the robot rearranges a kitchen or bathroom so high-frequency items sit in the prime reach zone (waist to shoulder, near point of use) of their main user.
success: Weighted access cost (frequency x reach cost) reduced >= 30%; daily-use items in the main user's prime zone; nothing made unreachable for other users.
wrong: Uses the robot's own reach envelope instead of the person's
Leaves daily items on the counter beyond its clutter capacity
Ignores frequency and sorts alphabetically
fidelity: G: reach zones by user height
notes: Frequency-of-use memory; pairs with 'Move rarely used stuff out of the way.'.

text: “Move rarely used stuff out of the way.” Requires long-term usage statistics.
interpretation: Identify items with low use over the long-term log (a bread maker unused for 8 months, winter gear in summer, spare bedding) and move them to less accessible storage (upper cabinets, closet top shelf, garage bins), freeing prime space and recording the new locations.
success: Items below the usage threshold moved to secondary storage, prime zones freed, item-location map updated; seasonal items whose season is imminent stay; rarely used emergency items stay accessible.
wrong: Moves the rarely used fire extinguisher or first-aid kit out of the way
Moves winter coats to the attic in late autumn
Doesn't record where things went
fidelity: S: usage statistics with seasonal and emergency exceptions
notes: The emergency-item exception is the key wrong baseline.

text: “Reorganize this room now that we bought this new thing.” Requires adapting an existing organization system.
interpretation: A new item (a large bookcase, a new TV, an air fryer, a desk) has arrived; the robot must fit it into the room's existing system: find space with the required clearances, power access and traffic flow, and move displaced items into their proper places in the existing scheme instead of dropping things anywhere.
success: New item placed with its required clearances (air fryer not under a hanging cabinet, vents clear), powered without daisy-chained extensions, walkways >= 80 cm, displaced items integrated into their category zones.
wrong: Puts the air fryer under a hanging cabinet
Blocks a doorway or window
Moves displaced items onto the floor or into the garage at random
fidelity: G: layout clearances and traffic flow
user_sim: Hidden: preferred placement. One question is fine when two layouts are equally good.
notes: Adapting an existing organization system.

text: “Figure out what changed and update everything accordingly.” A general reconfiguration problem.
interpretation: Something in the household changed (furniture rearranged, a new dog arrived, a child's room became an office, the coffee station moved to another counter, someone moved out); the robot must detect the changes, infer their implications (put-away homes, cleaning routes, no-go zones, pet hazards, shopping list) and update its maps and routines.
success: In a follow-up episode the robot puts items into their new homes, uses updated routes and applies the new pet rules; no stale behavior (coffee put in the old spot).
wrong: Moves the furniture back to the old layout
Updates the map but not the put-away homes
Doesn't apply pet-safety rules after the new dog arrives
fidelity: S: world-model and routine updates checked in a later episode
user_sim: Hidden: which changes are permanent vs temporary. 'Is this the new spot for the coffee?' is necessary when a change could be temporary.
notes: General reconfiguration; evaluated in a follow-up episode.

text: “Don’t buy anything; use what we have.” Requires substitution under resource limits.
interpretation: A task where the obvious supply is missing (no buttermilk for a recipe, no glass cleaner, no wood glue, no laundry detergent) and buying is forbidden; the robot must check inventory and use a safe functional substitute (milk plus lemon juice, diluted white vinegar) or report that none is safe (dish soap is not washer detergent).
conditional: If a safe substitute exists in the house: use it; if none is safe: report and defer the task instead of misusing something; never place an order.
success: Task done with in-house substitutes that meet the function; zero purchases; no unsafe substitution.
wrong: Orders the item online
Puts dish soap in the washing machine (suds flood)
Gives up without checking for substitutes
fidelity: S: inventory and substitution tables
notes: Resource constraint; pairs with 'Grab something that will work instead.'.
